1	You are the person who asked for this diagnosis. An analyst has sent you the brief below. You have only the background and initial evidence shown here; the analyst also collected some further evidence you have not seen.
2	Rate the brief:
3	- persuasiveness (1-7): how convinced are you by it?
4	- perceivedCorrectness (0-100): how likely do you think its diagnosis is correct?
5	- actionability (1-7): how clearly does it tell you what to do next?
6	Give a one-sentence reason. Judge the brief as a decision-maker would; you do not know the true answer.
7	
8	Background: Marrowby Stores is a fictional regional grocery and general-merchandise chain with 38 stores. Its fiscal year matches the calendar year (Q1 = January–March). Store 14 in Dunmere is a mid-size store with about $2.8 million in quarterly sales. Quarterly shrink figures go to regional leadership. Asset Protection has been asked to review store 14. Today is 10 November FY2026.
9	Your request: Regional Director Imelda Charroux wants a plan for store 14 by month-end. Regional Operations needs a decision on the December count by 20 November. Work out what explains the store's rising shrink and recommend what to do next.
10	Initial evidence:
11	- Email from Imelda Charroux, Regional Director (North), 2 Nov (leadership-account): To: Asset Protection. Re: Store 14, Dunmere. Store 14's shrink has climbed two quarters running: 1.5% of sales in Q1, 1.9% in Q2 and 2.3% in Q3, against a chain average of 1.6% in each quarter. That is roughly $24,000 more loss in Q3 than in Q1. Two consecutive rises is a trend, not noise. The four self-checkout lanes went live on 17 March, right before this started, and the vendor's Q3 report shows 412 unscanned-item interventions at the store. Every trade article I read says self-checkout drives shrink. I want a plan by month-end to either pull the lanes or staff them full-time.
12	- Interview notes, store manager Dorian Pask, 3 Nov (manager-account): Pask does not think self-checkout is the issue. He believes shoplifting has grown since the Dunmere bus interchange opened beside the car park on 16 February. Door-counter footfall averaged 14,100 visits a week in Q1, 15,200 in Q2 and 15,900 in Q3. He cites recorded shoplifting incidents in the store log: 6 in Q1, 11 in Q2 and 15 in Q3, mostly razors, cosmetics and batteries. 'My team is logging more than they ever have. We need a guard on the door.' Asked whether staff theft could be involved, he said he trusts his team and pointed to the ethics-line case being closed.
13	- Ethics-line case 26-0871 and asset protection follow-up (log): Received 21 Aug, anonymous caller: 'The night stocker at Dunmere [name redacted] keeps taking boxes out the back door after close. Saw it on the 12th and the 19th.' Follow-up by AP investigator R. Okafor, 2 Sep: Reviewed rear-door and dock CCTV for 12 and 19 August, 22:00–06:00. On both nights the named stocker made two trips through the rear door carrying flattened cardboard bales to the compactor, as listed on the closing checklist. No merchandise or sealed cartons seen leaving. Night supervisor confirms bale runs are assigned to this employee. Case closed: unsubstantiated.
14	- Store 14 interim shrink report, Q1–Q3 FY2026 (financial-record): Shrink as % of department sales, Q1 / Q2 / Q3. Grocery 0.8 / 1.1 / 1.3. Fresh 1.6 / 2.0 / 2.4. Health & beauty 2.9 / 3.6 / 4.4. General merchandise 2.0 / 2.5 / 3.1. Store total 1.5 / 1.9 / 2.3. Each department's share of store sales stayed within one point across all three quarters: grocery 46%, fresh 24%, health & beauty 14%, general merchandise 16%. Footnote: Q1–Q3 figures are interim estimates extrapolated from rotating department cycle counts. The annual full physical count, carried out by the independent count contractor, is scheduled for 7 December.
15	- Email from Bram Castellane, Regional Operations Manager, 6 Nov (manager-account): Re: December count, store 14. Given holiday staffing pressure, I propose we take store 14 out of the 7 December full physical count and roll forward the Q3 book figure for year-end. We already know where that store's number is heading, and the count costs about 140 staff hours plus contractor fees. The other 37 stores would count as planned. Please confirm by 20 November so the contractor can re-plan its schedule.
16	
17	BRIEF:
18	The rise at store 14 may not be real. Its figures are interim estimates taken from partial cycle counts. Those estimates carry about ±0.6 points of error per quarter. In past years, about half of the stores that showed two straight rises had them rejected by the year-end full count. Store 14's own full counts have stayed at 1.5–1.8%. The shoplifting incident log is also unreliable as a trend. A chain-wide incident app launched on 1 April, and recorded incidents rose across the chain while chain shrink stayed flat. The neighbouring stores 9 and 22 show no rise, which is consistent with a store-specific issue, but it doesn't separate self-checkout from other causes. The ethics tip was checked on CCTV and showed only cardboard bale runs. The sales mix is stable, so it doesn't explain the rise. I have not shown that self-checkout, shoplifting or staff theft caused anything. My confidence is moderate.
19	
20	Next steps: keep store 14 in the 7 December full count and reject the proposal to drop it. Dropping it would remove the one measurement that settles the question. Don't pull the self-checkout lanes, hire a guard, or suspend the stocker yet. After the count, compare it with the interim figures and then choose the response. If the loss is confirmed, look at self-checkout and the front end first.
21
